{"id": "73:20/q17", "question": "What does the command to seek forgiveness call for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "73:20/q17/p1", "position": "Believers should seek forgiveness for sins and shortcomings.", "reasons": "IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (author): God turned toward them with forgiveness and lightened the requirement. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The command seeks forgiveness for sins and shortcomings, especially those in night vigil. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (مقاتل): The alternative view takes God's forgiveness here to concern those who persist in sin; Muqatil argues this better establishes praise than a promise only to the repentant. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The command means to ask God to forgive one's sins. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): Seek God's forgiveness in all circumstances because no person is free of shortcomings. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): Ask forgiveness for sins and for falling short in good works. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Seek God’s forgiveness often in every affair, since He forgives and shows mercy to those who ask. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): The sūra closes with seeking forgiveness for the disbelievers' earlier resistance and for what obedient believers fail to fulfill, as 73:20 indicates. | mentions 73:20 BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): Calling the relief repentance does not imply a prior sin; the heavy obligation could have led people into sin. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): The surah's ending returns to its opening: encouragement to act and its reward recall the command to stand before God, while seeking forgiveness stresses the greatness of His station. | mentions 73:2 BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): End deeds by seeking forgiveness: even praised worship can produce self-admiration, and no one can render God His due, so servants must acknowledge shortcomings. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Seek God's forgiveness continually, at every time and in every condition, because people seldom escape negligence or shortcoming. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (السلف الصالح): The righteous early Muslims prayed until dawn, then sat seeking forgiveness until the dawn prayer. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): He recommends formulas of forgiveness drawn from Quranic divine names, including 'I ask forgiveness of God, for God is Oft-Returning' and 'O Lord, forgive and show mercy.' BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Knowing that God's forgiveness is not daunted by any sin should make a person ask forgiveness more often; the request is sound with humility, complete with repentance, and empty without either. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): He says writing the master formula of forgiveness and giving it to someone struggling to die will loosen the person's tongue and ease death, a remedy he says has been tried repeatedly. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): He gives the master formula: acknowledge God as Lord and creator, affirm servitude and covenant, seek refuge from one's deeds, confess favors and sin, and ask forgiveness from God alone. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Seek forgiveness in every state, since people rarely avoid shortcomings relative to their own standing. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): It is suggested that this is why the command to seek forgiveness follows the commands to pray, give zakat, and lend God a good loan. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Omitting the object of “forgiving” and “merciful” indicates that the forgiveness and mercy extend generally. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Believers should seek God's forgiveness in all circumstances because He is forgiving and merciful and grants the supplicant success through His mercy. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The closing supplication asks God to forgive and show mercy to the author and the believers who preceded them in faith, by the sanctity of what He revealed to His Messenger. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): When تاب means accepting repentance, it takes على by implication of مِن; when it means turning away from and regretting sin, it takes a preposition suited to that sense. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The waw begins an explanatory resumption: after easing night prayer, God directs believers to seek forgiveness in the night’s late hours as another devotional practice. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Late-night forgiveness seeking accords with 51:18 and with two Prophetic reports about the last third of the night and waking from sleep. | mentions 51:18 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet reports that each night, in its final third, God calls for people to pray, ask, or seek forgiveness, promising response, giving, and forgiveness. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet says that one who wakes at night, recites the stated remembrance, and then asks forgiveness or supplicates will have the request answered. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): God’s great forgiveness and mercy explain the command to seek forgiveness and encourage it as likely to be answered; the intensive descriptions hint at that promise. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): A distinct usage is God's return to people after their repentance, whose effect is forgiveness of their sins. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The closing command is to seek God's forgiveness; His description as forgiving and merciful intimates a promise of pardon and mercy. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The author allows that seeking forgiveness may mean performing all acts of obedience, since they are means to God's forgiveness. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (علي): Ali's hadith of the four hundred advises frequent seeking of forgiveness to attract provision and advancing whateve

{"id": "73:20/q18", "question": "What do God's forgiveness and mercy entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "73:20/q18/p1", "position": "God forgives and shows mercy to those who seek Him.", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Seeking forgiveness means asking God to forgive; He covers sins, pardons, and shows mercy. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (مقاتل): Muqatil holds that God is forgiving of all sins, including those of persistent sinners; the wording includes both repentant and persistent sinners, and forgiveness limited to penitents would be an obligatory act rather than praise. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The final description means God forgives believers' sins and is merciful to them. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (سعيد بن جبير): Sa'id ibn Jubayr says God forgives what preceded repentance and shows mercy to people afterward. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): God is forgiving and merciful. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): God is merciful by easing matters for those who exert themselves in worship. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): God's forgiveness covers sins and their effects until no blame or punishment remains; His mercy then adds generous honor and favor. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Ghafur forgives sins other than associating partners with God, while Rahim turns bad deeds into good deeds. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (عين المعاني): Ayn al-Maʻani glosses Ghafur as covering the failings of the ignorant and negligent, and Rahim as easing their burden. TAB-FULL: God forgives repentant servants and mercifully does not punish them. MAWARDI-FULL: God forgives what preceded repentance. MAWARDI-FULL: Sa'id says God shows mercy after repentance. WAHIDI-BASIT: Muqatil says God forgives and has mercy on believers. WAHIDI-BASIT: Ibn Abbas says God forgives those not persisting in sin."}]}
{"id": "73:20/q19", "question": "When and where was this closing passage revealed?", "turns_on": "The sources differ in the readings, referents, chronology, legal scope, or explanation shown by the positions.", "positions": [{"id": "73:20/q19/p1", "position": "The closing passage was revealed in Mecca.", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Another view says prayer and zakat were already obligatory in Mecca, so the verse is Meccan. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar found a Meccan youth who regularly attended the mosque selling food; he urged him toward livestock, saying food sellers welcome scarcity while herders welcome rain. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): The dual and third fractions are accusative for Makkan and Kufan readers, linked to adnā; those reading them genitive link them to “two thirds.” IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): God foreknows that illness, travel for livelihood, and fighting in His path will excuse some Muslims from night vigil; since this Meccan surah preceded legislation of fighting, the prediction is a sign of prophethood. ITQAN, d. 911 (ابن الغرس): Ibn al-Ghars reports a view that the passage beginning “Your Lord knows” through the end of al-Muzzammil is Meccan. | mentions 73:20 ITQAN, d. 911 (author): Al-Suyuti rejects the view that the ending is Meccan, citing Aisha's report that it was revealed later when night prayer was made obligatory. | mentions 73:20 ITQAN, d. 911 (author): Al-Suyuti prefers the agreed Meccan example: the night prayer commanded at the start of al-Muzzammil was abrogated by its end or by the five daily prayers. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAtiyya says the majority considered the sura Makkan except 73:20 to its end; al-Qurtubi attributes the same view to al-Thaʿlabi. | mentions 73:20 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (صاحب الإتقان): The Itqan author cites al-Hakim from ʿAʾisha: the ending was revealed a year after the opening, when night vigil had been imposed before the five prayers, implying the whole sura was Makkan. | mentions 73:20 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (عائشة): Some of ʿAʾisha's reports imply the entire sura is Makkan and its ending came a year after its opening, before obligatory prayer, as transmitted by al-Hakim via the Itqan author. | mentions 73:20 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Early authorities differed over when and where this verse was revealed and how its ruling relates to the preceding verse; the trusted view is that the opening was Makkan. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Reports place this Meccan verse eight months, a year, or ten years after the sura's opening verses. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The claim that Meccan zakat was imposed without specifying thresholds is unsupported."}, {"id": "73:20/q19/p2", "position": "The closing passage was revealed in Medina.", "reasons": "BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Since the Prophet was present when this verse was revealed, the travelers were not leaving him for instruction; if the surah's ending is Medinan, they could instead be migrating to Medina for learning. The rule also serves later generations. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (من فسرها بالزكاة المفروضة): Those who read this as obligatory zakat regard the sura's final passage as Medinan, treating its ruling as one whose legislation followed its revelation. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (أبو حيان): Some scholars call the verse Medinan; Abu Hayyan describes that as the majority position, but Elmalılı says it does not appear to be the majority view.
